meta.description: AI-focused regulatory dataset: worldwide laws, regulations, and frameworks that carry binding AI-specific provisions, plus the major voluntary AI governance frameworks. Each entry's `trigger` is evaluated against user answers to assign a tier.

tiers.baseline: Applies to essentially every business — surface always.
tiers.applies: Definite match based on answers — in scope now.
tiers.pending: In scope but obligations not yet effective (future date).
tiers.verify: Probable match — flag for professional review, do not assert certainty.
tiers.watch: Not yet applicable; monitor for passage or effective date.
tiers.recommend: Voluntary framework — recommended given the profile.

trigger_grammar.any: list of {q, in} conditions — TRUE if ANY match
trigger_grammar.all: list of conditions — TRUE only if ALL match
trigger_grammar.in: list of answer ids; TRUE if user's answer(s) intersect this list
trigger_grammar.tier_if: overrides default tier when a condition holds (e.g. pending until effective date)

meta.scope_note: AI-only. Includes (a) AI-native laws, (b) privacy/sector laws with binding AI provisions (profiling/ADM, deepfakes, health/payment AI), and (c) major voluntary AI frameworks. Excludes general cybersecurity/privacy rules with no AI-specific provision, and non-binding national AI strategies. Curated, not exhaustive; verify against primary sources.

types.sectoral: AI in a specific sector (employment, health, payments)
types.data_adm: Privacy law with automated-decision / profiling rules
types.framework: Voluntary AI governance framework or standard

laws.name: Health Insurance Portability & Accountability Act
laws.scope: Healthcare providers, health plans, clearinghouses, and all business associates.
laws.smb: Required for any healthcare SMB or any vendor touching protected health information.
ai: Any AI tool processing PHI requires a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA).
Training AI on patient data requires de-identification (Safe Harbor or Expert Determination).
AI diagnostic tools may qualify as FDA-regulated medical devices — dual compliance.
Automated clinical decisions must comply with the minimum necessary standard.
laws.enf: HHS/OCR — up to $1.93M per year per violation category.
laws.act: Get a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA) from every AI vendor that touches PHI before you use their tool.

laws.name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
laws.scope: Services directed at children under 13, or knowingly collecting data from children.
laws.smb: Relevant for EdTech, gaming, parenting, or entertainment SMBs.
ai: AI recommendation and personalization on children's platforms face strict parental consent rules.
AI behavioral profiling of children for targeting is heavily restricted.
FTC's 2024 enforcement increasingly targets AI-driven data collection and personalization.
Proposed COPPA 2.0 would extend protections to age 16 — monitor Congressional progress.
laws.enf: FTC — up to $51,744 per violation.
laws.act: Run an age-verification and parental-consent review on any AI product you offer to consumers.

laws.name: FTC Act Section 5 — Unfair or Deceptive Acts
laws.scope: All US businesses — universal catch-all for privacy and AI consumer harms.
laws.smb: Applies to every SMB using AI — this is your baseline liability exposure, regardless of size.
ai: FTC has pursued companies for deceptive claims about AI capabilities, safety, and data practices.
Privacy policies must accurately and completely describe all AI data-processing activities.
AI-generated content that deceives consumers about its origin is a direct enforcement target.
Algorithmic discrimination causing consumer harm qualifies as an unfair practice.
laws.enf: FTC — injunctions and civil penalties. Note: AMG Capital Mgmt. v. FTC (2021) held that Section 13(b) does not authorize disgorgement/restitution in direct federal court actions; monetary relief now requires the administrative cease-and-desist process under Sections 5/19.
laws.act: Audit your own privacy policy and any AI marketing claims for accuracy — this is the FTC's most common enforcement angle.

laws.name: California Consumer Privacy Act / Privacy Rights Act (CCPA/CPRA)
laws.scope: Businesses with $25M+ revenue, 100K+ CA consumer records, or 50%+ revenue from data sales — serving CA residents.
laws.smb: Gold standard for US state law — most SMBs with CA customers should treat it as a compliance floor.
laws.tier_reason: Coverage depends on revenue/volume thresholds — confirm the business meets one.
ai: Right to opt out of Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) — regulations finalized 2024.
Consumers can request human review of significant AI-driven decisions.
AI profiling and behavioral advertising require opt-out mechanisms and clear disclosure.
Sensitive data (biometrics, health, precise geolocation) has heightened AI use restrictions.
Data minimization and purpose limitation apply to all AI training data collection.
laws.enf: CPPA + CA AG — $2,500 per violation; $7,500 per intentional violation.
laws.act: Add Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) opt-out and AI-use disclosure language to your privacy notice.

laws.name: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act
laws.scope: Businesses processing TX residents' personal data in a household/individual context. Excludes employee and B2B data. Small businesses (per SBA) largely exempt but still barred from selling sensitive data without consent.
laws.smb: Broad reach with no revenue/volume threshold — but note the employment and B2B carve-outs.
laws.tier_reason: SBA small-business exemption may apply; sensitive-data sale ban still applies regardless of size.
ai: No revenue or volume threshold — broadly applicable, but only to consumer (not employee/B2B) data.
Right to opt out of targeted advertising, data sales, and AI profiling for consequential decisions.
Biometric and health data require opt-in consent before use in AI systems.
Data protection assessments required for AI processing with heightened privacy risk.
laws.enf: TX AG — up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.act: Confirm whether your data is consumer-context (in scope) or employee/B2B (excluded) before assuming this applies to you.

laws.name: Colorado Privacy Act
laws.scope: Controllers processing 100K+ CO consumers/year, or 25K+ with data-sale revenue.
laws.smb: The comprehensive privacy baseline for CO customers; pairs with the separate CO ADMT law.
laws.tier_reason: Coverage depends on the 100K-consumer / 25K-with-sales thresholds.
ai: Right to opt out of profiling for decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
Data protection assessments required for high-risk AI profiling.
Universal opt-out signal recognition required.
Opt-in consent required for sensitive data used in AI systems.
laws.enf: CO AG — up to $20,000 per violation.
laws.act: Prepare a data protection assessment for any AI profiling you run on Colorado consumers.

laws.name: Colorado AI Act — SB 26-189 (Automated Decision-Making Technology)
laws.scope: Developers and deployers of ADMT used in consequential decisions affecting CO residents. Replaces the repealed SB 24-205 with a transparency-focused framework.
laws.smb: The US AI-governance bellwether — effective Jan 1, 2027. Narrower than the repealed SB 205 (no duty of care), focused on disclosure and appeal rights.
laws.tier_reason: SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027; SB 24-205 was repealed and never took effect.
ai: Regulates ADMT in consequential decisions (employment, credit, insurance, housing, education).
Removes the repealed SB 205's duty-of-care and broad risk-management framework.
Developers must give deployers documentation sufficient for compliance.
Deployers must notify consumers of ADMT use and provide appeal/reconsideration.
3-year record retention; AG enforcement under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act.
laws.enf: CO AG under CCPA — violations treated as deceptive trade practices.
laws.act: Start building your ADMT disclosure and appeal process now — SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027, and this is a national bellwether other states are likely to follow.

laws.name: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.scope: Controllers processing 100K+ VA consumers/year, or 25K+ generating 50%+ data-sale revenue.
laws.smb: GDPR-aligned structure — mastering VCDPA unlocks most other state frameworks.
laws.tier_reason: Coverage depends on the 100K / 25K-with-sales thresholds.
ai: Right to opt out of profiling for targeted advertising, data sales, and significant decisions.
Data protection assessments required for high-risk AI profiling with significant legal effects.
Controller/processor structure mirrors GDPR — if you're already GDPR-compliant, adapting is quick.
Opt-in consent required for sensitive data categories used in AI systems.
laws.enf: VA AG — up to $7,500 per intentional violation.
laws.act: If you're building a multi-state privacy program, VCDPA's GDPR-aligned structure is a good baseline to start from.

laws.name: Other US State Comprehensive Privacy Laws
laws.scope: CT, MT, UT, IA, NH, NJ, TN, IN, OR, DE and others — 13+ states in effect by end of 2025.
laws.smb: Track which states your customers are in — the patchwork is expanding fast.
laws.tier_reason: Applicability and thresholds vary by state; confirm each based on customer geography.
ai: All follow the VCDPA model: opt-out rights, data protection assessments, controller/processor roles.
Most include AI profiling restrictions for decisions with significant legal or financial effects.
Thresholds vary but converge around 100K consumers/year.
Federal privacy law remains stalled — the state patchwork will keep expanding.
laws.enf: Varies — typically $5K–$20K per violation, enforced by state AG.
laws.act: Map which states your customers are in — this patchwork is expanding fast, and each state sets its own thresholds.

laws.name: Connecticut Data Privacy Act (as amended by PA 25-113)
laws.scope: Controllers doing business in CT or targeting CT residents. As of July 1, 2026: 35K-consumer threshold (down from 100K), OR any processing of sensitive data, OR any sale of personal data — the last two with no volume threshold.
laws.smb: The 2026 amendments dramatically widen coverage — any SMB touching sensitive data or selling data is now in scope regardless of size.
laws.tier_reason: In scope if processing sensitive data or selling data (no threshold), or 35K+ consumers — confirm which trigger applies.
ai: Effective July 1, 2026: threshold lowered to 35K; new no-threshold triggers for sensitive data and any data sale.
Sensitive data expanded to include neural data and government ID numbers; opt-in consent required.
New LLM-training disclosure: controllers must disclose if personal data is used to train large language models.
Profiling opt-out expanded to decisions involving human review, not just solely-automated ones.
Data Protection & Impact Assessments now explicitly cover AI profiling and consequential decisions.
laws.enf: CT AG — exclusive enforcement, no private right of action; up to $5,000 per willful violation.
laws.act: Re-check your CT coverage as of July 1, 2026 — the sensitive-data and data-sale triggers have no volume threshold, so you may be newly in scope even if you weren't before.

laws.name: Illinois HB 3773 — AI in Employment
laws.scope: Employers of any size with employees in Illinois, or hiring in Illinois, using AI in employment decisions. Amends the Illinois Human Rights Act (775 ILCS 5/2-102(L)).
laws.smb: Applies to any size employer with even one IL employee — covers ATS, video interview analysis, and performance AI.
ai: Effect-based liability: unlawful to use AI that results in discrimination, even if unintentional.
Prohibits using zip codes as a proxy for protected classes.
Notice requirement: employers must tell employees/applicants when AI is used in covered decisions.
Covers recruitment, hiring, promotion, discipline, discharge, tenure, and conditions of employment.
IDHR to issue implementing rules on notice timing and method (draft rules issued Dec 2025).
laws.enf: Illinois Dept. of Human Rights — IHRA complaint process; damages, penalties, fees, injunctive relief (no fixed per-violation cap).
laws.act: Audit your HR systems for AI components, and put a notice procedure and disparate-impact review in place before you use them on Illinois employees or applicants.

laws.name: Tennessee ELVIS Act (Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security)
laws.scope: Protects any individual's name, photograph, voice, or likeness — including AI-generated voice clones and deepfakes. Amends TN's Personal Rights Protection Act (Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-25-1101 et seq.).
laws.smb: Relevant to any SMB in music, media, entertainment, or generative AI — and to platforms/tools that distribute or enable synthetic voice/likeness.
ai: Covers AI-generated voice clones and visual deepfakes explicitly — 'voice' includes simulations.
Secondary liability: platforms and tool providers liable for distributing or enabling unauthorized use.
Liability for distributing an algorithm/tool whose primary purpose is producing a person's voice/likeness.
Fair-use (news/sports/public affairs) exemption narrowed to First-Amendment-protected uses.
Applies to deceased individuals' rights (heirs/executor have standing).
laws.enf: Civil action; statutory damages; remedies explicitly cumulative with other law.
laws.act: If your business touches voice cloning, deepfakes, or synthetic media, assess your exposure — and your vendors' — under this law before you ship.

laws.name: Utah Artificial Intelligence Policy Act (as amended 2025)
laws.scope: Entities using generative AI to interact with Utah consumers. 2025 amendments (SB 226, SB 332) narrowed the disclosure duty and extended the sunset to July 1, 2027.
laws.smb: Narrower than the 2024 original — disclosure now required only on clear request, or for high-risk interactions in regulated occupations.
ai: 2025 SB 226 narrowed disclosure: required only on a clear and unambiguous consumer request.
Regulated occupations (licensed professions) must disclose only for 'high-risk AI interactions'.
Safe harbor if the GenAI itself clearly discloses it is non-human at the outset and throughout.
'Generative AI' redefined more narrowly (systems designed to simulate human conversation).
Companion laws: HB 452 (mental-health chatbots), SB 271 (AI deepfake identity protection).
laws.enf: Utah Division of Consumer Protection — up to $2,500 admin fine per violation; AG civil penalties up to $5,000.
laws.act: If you run a chatbot for Utah consumers, have it clearly disclose it's not human at the outset — that alone qualifies you for the safe harbor.

laws.name: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (HB 149)
laws.scope: Use and development of AI systems connected to Texas. Amends the Business & Commerce Code with prohibited-use bans, a regulatory sandbox, and an AI Council. Broad, technology-neutral definition of an AI system.
laws.smb: Applies to businesses using or developing AI that touches Texas. The core exposure for most SMBs is the prohibited-use bans and the intent-based standard.
ai: Bans AI built to manipulate behavior, incite self-harm or crime, or produce unlawful deepfake CSAM.
Prohibits AI intended to unlawfully discriminate against protected classes.
Prohibits government social-scoring and certain biometric identification without consent.
Creates a regulatory sandbox and an AI Council; enforcement is intent-based.
laws.enf: Texas Attorney General — exclusive enforcement, with a cure period; civil penalties per violation (higher for uncurable/continued violations). No private right of action.
laws.act: Review your AI uses against TRAIGA's prohibited-use list and document that none are designed for the banned purposes before Jan 1, 2026.

laws.name: California Transparency in Frontier AI Act (SB 53 / TFAIA)
laws.scope: Large 'frontier' AI developers training models above very high compute thresholds. The first US law addressing catastrophic-risk frontier model safety; obligations fall on the biggest developers, not deployers.
laws.smb: Almost no SMB is a covered frontier developer — this applies to the largest AI labs. Included so you can confirm it does NOT apply to you, and understand the frontier-safety baseline.
laws.tier_reason: Only 'large frontier developers' (models trained above ~10^26 FLOPs) are covered — effectively no SMB qualifies; shown for awareness.
ai: Applies only to large frontier developers training above extreme compute thresholds.
Covered developers must publish a frontier AI safety framework and risk assessments.
Critical safety incidents must be reported to California's Office of Emergency Services.
Adds whistleblower protections for frontier-lab employees.
laws.enf: California Attorney General — civil penalties for covered large frontier developers that fail to publish or report as required.
laws.act: Unless you train frontier-scale models, this does not apply — confirm you are below the threshold and move on.

laws.name: California Generative AI Training Data Transparency Act (AB 2013)
laws.scope: Developers of generative AI systems made available to Californians. Requires public documentation of the datasets used to train the system.
laws.smb: Applies if you develop or substantially modify a generative AI system offered to people in California — not if you only use someone else's AI tool.
laws.tier_reason: Applies to developers/substantial modifiers of generative AI, not to businesses that merely use a third-party tool; confirm which role you play.
ai: Developers must post a public, high-level summary of the datasets used to train the model.
Documentation must cover data sources, whether data includes personal information, and copyright status.
Applies to generative AI released or substantially modified for Californians.
Using a vendor's AI tool without modifying it generally keeps you out of scope.
laws.enf: Enforced under California law; the practical risk is non-compliant public documentation and follow-on unfair-practice exposure.
laws.act: If you train or substantially fine-tune a generative model offered in California, prepare the public training-data documentation this law requires.

laws.name: New York RAISE Act (Responsible AI Safety and Education Act)
laws.scope: Large frontier AI developers operating in or serving New York. Safety, disclosure, and incident-reporting duties focused on catastrophic risk — similar in spirit to California SB 53.
laws.smb: Like the California frontier law, this targets the largest developers, not typical deployers or SMBs. Included for awareness and to confirm non-applicability.
laws.tier_reason: Takes effect January 1, 2027 and covers only large frontier developers; not yet in force and not applicable to typical SMBs.
ai: Targets large frontier developers, not deployers or ordinary AI users.
Requires safety plans, disclosures, and reporting of critical safety incidents.
Focused on preventing catastrophic-risk scenarios from frontier models.
Effective January 1, 2027.
laws.enf: New York Attorney General — penalties for covered large developers; details set by the enacted text and any implementing guidance.
laws.act: Unless you are a frontier-scale developer, no action — note the 2027 date and confirm you are out of scope.

laws.name: US State Chatbot & Companion-AI Disclosure Laws
laws.scope: A growing cluster of state laws (California, Utah, and others) requiring that consumers be told when they are interacting with an AI chatbot rather than a human, with extra duties for companion and mental-health bots.
laws.smb: Directly relevant if you run any consumer-facing chatbot or virtual assistant. The common thread is a clear 'you're talking to AI' disclosure.
laws.tier_reason: The exact disclosure rules vary by state and by bot type (general, companion, mental-health); confirm which states' rules apply to your bot.
ai: Core requirement: clearly disclose to users that they are interacting with AI, not a person.
Companion and mental-health chatbots face heightened safety and referral duties in some states.
Disclosure timing (upfront vs. on request) varies by state.
The number of enacted chatbot-disclosure laws is growing each session.
laws.enf: State attorneys general and consumer-protection regulators — penalties vary by state statute.
laws.act: Add a clear 'you're chatting with an AI assistant' disclosure to every consumer-facing bot, and review companion/mental-health rules if your bot fits those categories.

laws.name: EU General Data Protection Regulation
laws.scope: Any organization offering goods/services to, or monitoring behavior of, EU/EEA data subjects — regardless of company location.
laws.smb: Applies to any SMB with EU customers, EU employees, or EU vendor data.
ai: Article 22: right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant legal effects.
Mandatory human-review option for AI-driven consequential decisions.
Valid legal basis required for AI training data (consent, legitimate interest, contract).
DPIAs required before deploying high-risk AI processing.
Right to explanation for automated decisions; US AI-tool transfers require SCCs or adequacy.
laws.enf: National DPAs — up to €20M or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
laws.act: Run a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) on any AI system that processes EU personal data, and confirm your US AI vendors have valid SCCs in place.

laws.name: UK GDPR + Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
laws.scope: Organizations processing UK residents' personal data. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 rewrote the automated-decision-making rules, diverging from the EU.
laws.smb: Treat as a separate obligation from EU GDPR — the 2025 Act changed the ADM framework materially.
ai: DUAA 2025 replaced Article 22 with new Articles 22A–22D (effective Feb 5, 2026).
Default FLIPPED from prohibition-first to permission-first for solely automated decisions.
Significant decisions still require safeguards: notice, explanation, human review, right to contest.
'Meaningful human involvement' and 'significant decision' await Secretary-of-State regulations and ICO guidance.
UK + EU operations now need separate ADM compliance frameworks — they have diverged.
laws.enf: ICO — up to £17.5M or 4% of global annual turnover.
laws.act: Don't assume EU GDPR compliance covers you in the UK — map your UK data flows separately under the new Articles 22A–22D.

laws.name: Canada PIPEDA (+ proposed AIDA / Bill C-27)
laws.scope: Private-sector organizations collecting, using, or disclosing personal information in commercial activities in Canada.
laws.smb: Active now for any SMB with Canadian customers; Bill C-27 would add AI-specific requirements.
ai: Meaningful consent is difficult when AI processing is complex or opaque to users.
Bill C-27 proposes the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) for high-impact AI systems.
AIDA would require risk assessments, monitoring, and record-keeping for high-impact AI.
Breach notification for significant risk applies to AI systems handling personal data.
laws.enf: OPC — up to CAD $100K (increasing significantly under proposed C-27).
laws.act: Keep an eye on Bill C-27/AIDA — if it passes, AI-specific risk assessment and record-keeping requirements will apply to high-impact AI systems.

laws.name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act
laws.scope: Providers and deployers of AI systems used in the EU — a risk-tiered framework applicable to any company globally.
laws.smb: Applies to any SMB deploying AI affecting EU users. Prohibited uses in force since Feb 2025; high-risk deadlines deferred by the Digital Omnibus.
ai: Four risk tiers: Unacceptable (banned), High-risk, Limited-risk, Minimal-risk.
Prohibited since Feb 2025: social scoring, manipulative AI, most real-time biometric surveillance.
Article 50 transparency (AI disclosure, content labeling) still takes effect August 2, 2026.
High-risk AI (Annex III) obligations DEFERRED to December 2, 2027 by the Digital Omnibus (Reg. EU 2026/1744).
High-risk AI in regulated products (Annex I) deferred to August 2, 2028.
General-Purpose AI (LLM) obligations in effect since August 2025.
laws.enf: National market surveillance authorities — up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover.
laws.act: Build an inventory of every AI system you use or offer to EU users, and classify each by risk tier now — the high-risk deadlines are deferred, not cancelled.

laws.name: South Korea AI Basic Act (Framework Act on AI Development and Trust)
laws.scope: Providers and deployers of AI affecting Korean users, including businesses outside Korea. Act No. 20676; a one-year enforcement grace period runs through 2026 before fines are generally applied.
laws.smb: Applies extraterritorially to any business offering AI products or services to people in South Korea. Heaviest obligations fall on 'high-impact' AI (healthcare, energy, public services) and generative AI.
laws.tier_reason: In force since Jan 22, 2026 with a grace period through 2026; confirm whether your use is 'high-impact' or generative (heavier duties) versus general.
ai: High-impact AI in critical sectors must provide risk management, human oversight, and user notice.
Generative AI outputs must be labeled/disclosed to users.
Foreign providers over a user threshold must appoint a domestic representative in Korea.
One-year grace period in 2026 defers most fines except for serious harm.
laws.enf: Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) — administrative fines up to KRW 30 million; fact-finding and penalties largely deferred during the 2026 grace period.
laws.act: If you serve users in South Korea, map whether your AI is 'high-impact' or generative, and prepare labeling and human-oversight controls before the grace period ends.

laws.name: Vietnam Law on Artificial Intelligence (Law No. 134/2025/QH15)
laws.scope: Research, development, provision, deployment, and use of AI systems connected to Vietnam. A risk-based framework with high / medium / low tiers and correspondingly stricter controls.
laws.smb: One of Southeast Asia's first comprehensive AI laws. Applies to businesses developing or deploying AI in or into Vietnam; obligations scale with the system's risk tier.
laws.tier_reason: In force since Mar 1, 2026; implementing decrees are still developing and obligations depend on your system's assigned risk tier.
ai: Three-tier risk system (high / medium / low) sets the level of regulatory control.
High-risk AI faces the strictest development, transparency, and oversight requirements.
Emphasis on AI infrastructure, data governance, and technological sovereignty.
Implementing decrees and technical detail are still being issued.
laws.enf: Vietnamese authorities under the AI Law and implementing decrees; specific penalty schedules are being finalized in secondary legislation.
laws.act: If you build or deploy AI touching Vietnam, classify your system by risk tier and watch the implementing decrees for concrete obligations.

laws.name: Japan AI Promotion Act (Act on Promotion of R&D and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies)
laws.scope: National framework promoting AI research, development, and use. Innovation-first: it sets principles and government coordination duties but imposes no direct penalties or binding obligations on private business.
laws.smb: Largely a promotional and coordination statute, not a compliance burden. Relevant as a signal of Japan's direction; obligations may come later through sector guidance.
laws.tier_reason: Promotional framework with no monetary penalties or direct private-sector obligations; monitor for follow-on sector-specific rules.
ai: Treats AI as a strategic national asset and promotes its development and use.
No monetary penalties and no direct binding duties on private companies.
Government may issue guidance and coordinate responses to AI-related harms.
Signals future direction; watch for sector regulators to add concrete rules.
laws.enf: No direct penalties — the Act relies on government guidance, cooperation, and coordination rather than enforcement.
laws.act: No immediate action if you operate in Japan; treat this as a signal and watch for sector-specific AI guidance built on top of it.

laws.name: Taiwan AI Basic Act
laws.scope: Sets national AI guiding principles and directs government bodies (Executive Yuan, MODA) to build a risk-classification framework. It does not itself impose obligations on the private sector.
laws.smb: No direct compliance duties for businesses yet. It frames Taiwan's approach and mandates future risk rules; the concrete obligations will come from MODA's forthcoming framework.
laws.tier_reason: The Basic Act sets principles only and imposes no private-sector obligations; watch MODA's risk-classification framework for actual duties.
ai: Codifies seven principles: well-being, human autonomy, privacy, security, transparency, fairness, accountability.
Directs MODA to develop an internationally aligned AI risk-classification framework.
Calls for high-risk AI application labeling and data openness with privacy by design.
No direct obligations on private business in the Basic Act itself.
laws.enf: No direct private-sector penalties in the Basic Act; enforcement will depend on the sector rules and risk framework that follow.
laws.act: If you operate in Taiwan, no action yet — watch MODA's risk-classification framework, which will carry the real obligations.

laws.name: China AI Rules (Generative AI, Deep Synthesis, Algorithm Recommendation & Labeling)
laws.scope: A cluster of binding CAC rules rather than one AI law: Algorithm Recommendation Provisions (2022), Deep Synthesis Provisions (2023), Generative AI Measures (2023), and AI content-labeling rules (2025).
laws.smb: Any business providing generative AI, recommendation, or synthetic-media services to users in mainland China is in scope. Content control, labeling, and security assessments are mandatory.
laws.tier_reason: Multiple overlapping CAC rules apply depending on service type (recommendation, deep synthesis, generative AI); confirm which rules and filings apply to you.
ai: Generative AI services require security assessments and algorithm filing with the CAC.
AI-generated and synthetic content must carry explicit and implicit labels (2025 rules).
Deep synthesis (deepfake) media requires consent, traceability, and labeling.
Recommendation algorithms must offer transparency and user opt-out controls.
laws.enf: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and related authorities — service suspension, takedowns, fines, and filing/registration requirements.
laws.act: If you offer generative, recommendation, or synthetic-media AI in mainland China, budget for CAC algorithm filing, security assessments, and content labeling.

laws.name: UAE AI Regulation (Dubai AI Act + DIFC Regulation 10)
laws.scope: A layered regime, not one horizontal statute: the Dubai AI Act (effective Mar 2026, ~10-month transition), DIFC Regulation 10 on autonomous/semi-autonomous systems (enforced Jan 2026), plus federal data-protection law and the National AI Strategy.
laws.smb: Relevant to businesses operating in Dubai or the DIFC free zone. The Dubai AI Act bans certain uses; DIFC Regulation 10 governs autonomous systems handling personal data.
laws.tier_reason: Obligations depend on where in the UAE you operate (Dubai, DIFC, or federal) and which layered instrument applies; confirm the applicable regime.
ai: Dubai AI Act prohibits social scoring, subliminal manipulation, workplace/education emotion recognition, and AI-only predictive policing.
DIFC Regulation 10 governs autonomous and semi-autonomous systems processing personal data.
UAE Central Bank guidance sets responsible-AI expectations for licensed financial institutions.
No single federal horizontal AI statute — obligations are spread across emirate and free-zone rules.
laws.enf: Dubai and DIFC authorities plus federal regulators — penalties and supervisory measures vary by the specific instrument and free zone.
laws.act: If you operate in Dubai or the DIFC, identify which layer applies to you and use the Dubai AI Act's prohibited-use list as a red-line checklist.

laws.name: Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225)
laws.scope: The first binding international AI treaty, tying AI to human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Obligations bind ratifying states, which then implement them in national law — it does not directly regulate businesses.
laws.smb: No direct business obligations. It matters as the backbone many countries (EU, UK, and others) will translate into their own enforceable AI laws over the next few years.
laws.tier_reason: A state-level treaty not yet in force (needs 5 ratifications); it shapes future national law rather than binding businesses today.
ai: First legally binding international treaty on AI and human rights.
Binds ratifying governments, which implement it through national legislation.
Signed by the EU, UK, US, Canada, Japan, and others; awaiting enough ratifications to enter into force.
A leading indicator of where signatory countries' AI laws are heading.
laws.enf: No direct enforcement against businesses — obligations run to ratifying states and surface later as national AI laws.
laws.act: No action today — track it as a preview of coming national AI rules in the countries where you operate.

laws.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
laws.scope: Voluntary — all organizations developing, deploying, or using AI. GenAI Profile (2024) covers LLMs.
laws.smb: The most widely referenced AI governance framework right now — a strong foundation for your AI security and governance program.
laws.tier_reason: Voluntary framework — recommended for any AI-using business.
ai: Four core functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE — a structured AI risk lifecycle.
Trustworthy AI properties: Accountable, Explainable, Fair, Privacy-enhanced, Reliable, Safe, Secure, Transparent.
GenAI Profile (2024) addresses LLM risks: hallucination, data poisoning, and misuse.
AI RMF Playbook provides 72 suggested actions mapped to each core function.
Referenced in federal contracts, insurance requirements, and litigation with increasing frequency.
laws.enf: Voluntary — increasingly required in contracts, federal programs, and litigation.
laws.act: Structure your AI risk management around the four core functions — GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE — even though this framework is voluntary; it's increasingly expected in contracts and litigation.

laws.name: ISO/IEC 42001 — AI Management System
laws.scope: Organizations developing, providing, or using AI — the first international AI management system standard.
laws.smb: Emerging market requirement — your enterprise customers will increasingly expect this certification if you're an AI-using vendor.
laws.tier_reason: Emerging voluntary standard — recommended for AI-using businesses anticipating enterprise requirements.
ai: First international standard for organizational AI management systems.
Covers AI policy, risk assessment, objectives, controls, and performance monitoring.
Annexes provide implementation guidance for AI use cases and impact assessments.
Certification track is emerging — likely to follow the ISO 27001 trajectory.
laws.enf: Certification-based — emerging contractual requirement in enterprise and regulated sectors.
laws.act: Map your AI practices against ISO 42001 now — it's the first international AI management standard, and enterprise customers will start requiring it.

laws.name: PCI DSS v4.0 — Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
laws.scope: Any organization that stores, processes, or transmits payment card data — mandatory by contract with card brands.
laws.smb: Applies to virtually every SMB that accepts cards; scope reduced when using a compliant third-party processor.
laws.tier_reason: Direct processing = full scope; third-party processor = reduced scope (SAQ), confirm the SAQ type.
ai: AI tools with access to cardholder data environments are in scope for PCI DSS.
Requirement 6.3 (vulnerability management) — AI-assisted scanning must produce compliant output.
Requirement 12.3 requires documented risk analysis for payment technologies — AI tools included.
Version 4.0 introduces a customized approach allowing AI-driven compensating controls.
laws.enf: Card brand penalties — fines, increased fees, and potential loss of ability to process payments.
laws.act: Make sure any AI tool with access to cardholder data is explicitly scoped into your PCI DSS assessment.

laws.name: OECD AI Principles
laws.scope: The first intergovernmental AI standard and the de facto global baseline — adopted by 47+ countries and referenced in the EU AI Act and US policy. Voluntary values-based principles for trustworthy AI.
laws.smb: A good, universally recognized starting point for an AI governance policy. Not enforceable itself, but aligning to it signals credibility and eases mapping to binding laws later.
laws.tier_reason: Voluntary intergovernmental principles — recommended as the common vocabulary underlying most national AI laws and frameworks.
ai: Five values-based principles: inclusive growth, human-centered values, transparency, robustness/safety, accountability.
The de facto global baseline — 47+ adopting countries and referenced in the EU AI Act and US executive policy.
A shared vocabulary that maps cleanly onto NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001.
Non-binding, but widely treated as the floor for 'responsible AI.'
laws.enf: Voluntary — no penalties. Value comes from credibility and from aligning early with the principles national laws are built on.
laws.act: Adopt the OECD AI Principles as the stated foundation of your AI policy — it aligns you with the baseline most binding laws share.

laws.name: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 — AI Risk Management Guidance
laws.scope: International guidance on managing AI-specific risk, designed to sit alongside ISO 42001 (the certifiable AI management system) and the general ISO 31000 risk approach.
laws.smb: The practical 'how to actually run AI risk management' companion to ISO 42001. Useful once you commit to a structured AI governance program.
laws.tier_reason: Voluntary international guidance — recommended as the operational risk-management companion to ISO 42001.
ai: Provides structured guidance for identifying, assessing, and treating AI-specific risks.
Aligns with ISO 31000 risk management and complements the ISO 42001 management system.
Guidance-only (not certifiable on its own), but concrete and operational.
Helps translate high-level AI principles into a working risk process.
laws.enf: Voluntary — no penalties; adopted to operationalize AI risk management and support ISO 42001 certification.
laws.act: Use ISO 23894 as the working risk-management method inside an ISO 42001 program rather than as a standalone target.

laws.name: G7 Hiroshima Process — International Code of Conduct for Advanced AI
laws.scope: A voluntary international code of conduct for organizations developing advanced/frontier AI systems, produced by the G7. Aimed at large developers of the most capable models.
laws.smb: Most relevant to organizations building advanced foundation models. For typical SMB AI users it is context, not an obligation.
laws.tier_reason: Voluntary and aimed at advanced/frontier AI developers; informational for most SMBs rather than an operational target.
ai: Voluntary code of conduct for developers of advanced/frontier AI systems.
Covers risk identification, security, transparency reporting, and content authentication.
Backed by G7 governments as part of the Hiroshima AI Process.
Feeds into national expectations for how frontier developers behave.
laws.enf: Voluntary — no penalties; influence comes through G7 government expectations and reputational signaling.
laws.act: Note it as context for advanced-AI norms; adopt its transparency practices only if you develop frontier-scale models.

laws.name: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
laws.scope: The first global standard on AI ethics, adopted by all UNESCO member states. A values framework that governments use to shape national policy; it does not bind businesses directly.
laws.smb: Background context rather than a compliance item. Useful vocabulary for an ethics policy, but not something you 'comply with' as a business.
laws.tier_reason: A member-state ethics recommendation with no direct business obligations; informational and useful as policy vocabulary.
ai: First global AI-ethics standard, adopted by all UNESCO member states.
Centers human rights, human dignity, environmental sustainability, and oversight.
Directed at governments to shape national policy, not at companies directly.
Useful language for an internal AI ethics statement.
laws.enf: No enforcement against businesses — it guides member states' policymaking.
laws.act: Draw on it for the ethics language in your AI policy; there is nothing to 'comply' with directly.

laws.name: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework (incl. Generative & Agentic AI)
laws.scope: Singapore's voluntary, practical AI governance framework, extended with dedicated guidance for generative AI and (in 2026) agentic AI, plus the AI Verify testing toolkit. Widely used across APAC.
laws.smb: One of the most practical, business-ready governance frameworks available — concrete and implementation-oriented. Voluntary, but a strong template even outside Singapore.
laws.tier_reason: Voluntary but unusually practical and business-ready; recommended as an implementation template, especially for APAC-facing SMBs.
ai: Practical, implementation-focused governance guidance rather than high-level principles.
Dedicated modules for generative AI and (2026) agentic AI systems.
Paired with AI Verify, a testing/assurance toolkit for AI systems.
Voluntary, but widely adopted as a template across Asia-Pacific.
laws.enf: Voluntary — no penalties; adopted for its practicality and as a credibility signal in APAC markets.
laws.act: Use Singapore's framework and AI Verify as a ready-made, concrete template when standing up your AI governance program.
